Such a method might consider factors like densities of populations/commercial development/industrial development/ institutional development by census tract, and might consider the volume and path of the flow of goods generated by each tract. Information was intensively sought from the Bureau of the Census, the Department of Transportation, the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the Department of Commerce, and various planning associations and organizations at national, regional, and local levels. While it is possible to capture or generate at certain cities some of the information that would be useful, there is no degree of uniformity in work already performed or needed by the different organizations/institutions which would justify the detailed development and implementation of the methods in mind. One of the stated purposes of this proceeding was to simplify. No suitable alternative to the population-mileage formula was found which would serve that purpose.
The use of Standard Metropolitan Statistical Areas to define C/Z's-T/A's is considered inappropriate for the reasons stated in the January 12, 1976, interim Report by the Commission in this proceeding on pages 163-164.
The application of a modified version of the Urbanized Area definitions which would allow greater distances than one and one-half miles between economically related communities meeting minimum and modified population density requirements perhaps offers the most promising alternative to use of a population-mileage formula. Most communities, however, would not meet the definition for Urbanized Areas. It is questionable as to whether or not such a method--modified as it would have to be--would be superior to a population-mileage formula for most municipalities. In any event, it would be very expensive to implement and maintain.
